title: What do candidates say about real consulting interviews?
description: Common themes from candidates' published interview experiences at MBB, the Big Four and Accenture: formats, surprises and lessons.
hook: Candidates who share their consulting interview experiences describe the same few patterns: formats are predictable, interviewers are usually more supportive than expected, fit questions catch out people who prepared only cases, and feedback and timelines vary a lot. The firms' own guidance backs most of this up. Treat individual stories as themes to practise, not a script of what you will be asked.
body:
Formats are fairly predictable

The firms say a good deal about their formats, and candidate reports mostly match:

  • McKinsey says that for most client-facing roles you will have problem-solving (case) interviews and a Personal Experience Interview, usually after its gamified Solve assessment. In the PEI you discuss one experience in depth, and McKinsey advises leading with your reasoning rather than a rehearsed story.
  • Bain says consulting applicants typically take a digital assessment and then case interviews, and that it asks all candidates for a role the same questions to reduce bias.
  • Accenture notes that an interviewer may spend the first half of the interview on your experience or go straight into the case.
  • Deloitte, in Australia for example, describes an assessment day that can include a group case study and a one-to-one interview with a leader.

So the surprise is rarely the format. It is the depth of follow-up questions. Our firm guides cover each process in detail, starting with McKinsey and Bain.

Interviewers are often kinder than expected

Many candidates describe interviewers as friendly and willing to guide them. Accenture's own advice says it plainly: the interviewer really wants you to do well. Oliver Wyman tells candidates to treat the interviewer as a client and work together. A hint is not a trap. Use it, say thank you, and move on.

Supportive does not mean easy. Interviewers push on numbers and assumptions, and that is where reports show candidates slipping. A typical exchange:

Candidate: "Revenue is $2.4M and margin fell from 20% to 15%, so profit fell 5%."
Interviewer: "Are you sure?"

Profit went from $2.4M × 20% = $480k to $2.4M × 15% = $360k. That is a fall of $120k, or 25%, not 5%. The margin fell 5 percentage points. A strong candidate catches it when asked, corrects it calmly and says what it means: "So profit fell by a quarter, which makes this urgent." How to get through case maths without mistakes covers the habits that prevent this.

Fit questions matter more than people expect

Candidates who prepared only cases often say the fit or experience questions were where they struggled. Interviewers dig: "What exactly did you say?" "What would you do differently?" "How did the other person react?" A story you have only summarised falls apart by the third question. Prepare six to eight stories with real detail, and practise being questioned on them. The fit interview guide shows how.

Feedback and timelines vary

Some processes move very fast: KPMG UK says successful graduate candidates hear within two working days of its final assessment. Others take weeks, and experienced-hire processes can run for months. Feedback is equally uneven. Some firms offer it on request, others give little. If you are rejected, ask politely; you may get a useful pointer. What to do after a rejection.

How to use other people's reports without overfitting

Reports are useful for learning the range of formats, common case types and how hard the follow-up questions are. They are poor predictors of the exact questions you will get. A recent graduate's account from one country may describe a completely different process from an experienced hire's elsewhere, and a case that circulated online may well have been retired.

When you read a report, pull out the behaviours, not the content:

  • Did the candidate have to clarify an unclear objective?
  • Was their arithmetic challenged?
  • Did the interviewer change direction without warning?
  • Did they have to recommend from incomplete data?

Then practise those behaviours on an unfamiliar case, not the same questions word for word. Be sceptical of claims about secret frameworks or guaranteed interviews.

Write your own debrief

Your own experiences are better evidence than anyone else's. After every real or practice interview, spend ten minutes on a one-page debrief while it is fresh:

QuestionExample note
What was I asked?Profitability case, regional bakery chain; leadership story
Where did I slow down?Second calculation; lost track of units
What data did I ask for?Costs by store; forgot to ask about competitors
What would I do differently?Write units next to every number; state the so-what after each result

After five or six debriefs, patterns appear. Those patterns tell you exactly what to practise next.

Practise now

1. Costs are $1.6M on revenue of $2M. Costs rise by 10%. By how much does profit fall?

Show the answer

Profit starts at $2M − $1.6M = $400k. Costs rise by $160k to $1.76M, so profit falls to $240k. That is a 40% fall in profit from a 10% rise in costs, because margins are thin. Saying that so-what out loud is what interviewers want.

2. You read that a firm "always" asks a particular airline case. How should you use that?

Show the answer

Do not memorise it. Note what the case tests (perhaps capacity maths and a pricing judgement), practise those skills on two or three different cases, and read how airlines make money so the context feels familiar whatever you are asked.

Where to practise next
